01 / The question

How can spatial interaction support design when the problem—and the designer’s intent—is still taking shape?

Why this matters

Ill-defined design problems evolve as people explore potential solutions. EnactiveCanvas turns a two-dimensional workspace into a way to organize fragments, revisit alternatives, and communicate context to an LLM. The system instantiates a spatial–cognitive design space connecting design cognition with spatial properties and actions.

02 / Contribution & method

My contribution

I contributed frontend and backend system design, connecting spatial canvas actions with context-aware AI generation.

Role & scope

My primary contribution was system design across the frontend and backend. I contributed to the interactive web system that connects canvas operations and note state with context-aware AI generation. This contribution centers on the system; the design-space framework and user-study findings described here belong to the collaborative research.

01Represent the workspace＋

Represent an evolving workspace

The HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend uses Fabric.js for notes, connections, dragging, selection, panning, and zooming. Note state includes content, position, type, and organizational properties for layers, ratings, and sub-canvases.

02Translate spatial actions＋

Translate spatial actions into AI requests

The Python/Flask backend combines operation-specific prompts with note content, intent, and spatial parameters. Direction and distance encode the perspective and degree of an idea variation.

03Make context visible＋

Make context part of the interaction

Visible notes or an explicit selection supply context for generation. Separate operations support divergence, convergence, merging, question answering, and reflection; generated text returns to the canvas as notes or responses.

The studies suggest support for exploration and ownership, alongside greater effort and difficulty reaching a final proposal.

Team-level studies; the findings do not establish improved creativity. My contribution focused on the system.

Explore the study & findings

The team evaluated EnactiveCanvas in a comparative lab study with 23 participants and a two-week deployment with three expert designers. Qualitative findings suggest support for divergent exploration, reflection, ownership, and intent formation. Participants also reported greater effort, a learning cost, and difficulty synthesizing a final proposal.

ChatGPT received higher ratings for immersion and whether the results were worth the effort. The study did not find differences in the remaining creativity-support dimensions, user-experience measures, or expert ratings of design outcomes. These findings do not establish that EnactiveCanvas improves creativity.

Explore the system figure

04 / The next question

How can a spatial workspace help people move from expanding ideas to a coherent outcome?

A direction to explore

A next design iteration could connect spatial exploration to focused synthesis while preserving unfinished branches and user ownership. Evaluating longer-term use would help distinguish first-use friction from sustained benefits; the existing study does not isolate spatial interaction from other system differences.

Sources & attribution

Source: Spatial–Cognitive Mappings for Ill-Defined Design with AI: A Design Space and Its Instantiation in EnactiveCanvas, supplied manuscript, Sections 4–7. Contribution scope confirmed by Tony; evaluation findings are team-level results.
